title: LLM Training
oneLiner: How a large language model is built: read an enormous amount of text, keep guessing the next word, and choose the right balance of model size and data.

what.html:
Pre-training is where an LLM learns almost everything it knows. It reads trillions of words and practises one task, predicting the next word, billions of times. No one labels anything: the text itself contains the answers. How well this works depends on the data (clean, varied, without repeats) and on scale, which follows surprisingly predictable rules.

Everyday versionReading a whole library with a bookmark that hides the next word. Guess, peek, adjust. After billions of guesses you've absorbed grammar, facts and style without a teacher.

why.html:
• It explains where a model's knowledge (and its mistakes) come from.
  • Data quality and duplicates directly affect what the model memorises.
  • Scaling rules decide how big a model is worth training, and on how much text.

how.title: Guess the next word
how.html: Every position in every sentence is a small test: given the words so far, what comes next? If the model gave the right word a 25% chance, its "surprise" is −ln 0.25 ≈ 1.39; training lowers it.

how.title: Left-to-right or fill-in-the-blank
how.html: Chat models predict the next word using only what came before (causal). BERT-style models hide words and use both sides (masked): good for understanding, not for writing.

how.title: Clean, varied data without repeats
how.html: Collect, clean, remove duplicates, then tokenize. Repeated text makes models memorise rather than learn, so near-copies are detected and dropped.

how.title: Words into pieces
how.html: Byte-pair encoding glues together the most common letter pairs again and again, so common words become one token and rare words are spelled from a few pieces.

how.title: Specialising a general model
how.html: Keep pre-training on medical or legal text to deepen knowledge there, far cheaper than starting from scratch.

how.title: Bigger is better, predictably
how.html: Loss drops smoothly as you add compute, with each tenfold increase buying a bit less. Because the curve is predictable, labs can plan huge training runs from small experiments.

how.title: Balance size and data
how.html: Training cost ≈ 6 × parameters × tokens. For a fixed budget, use about 20 tokens per parameter: a 70-billion-parameter model wants about 1.4 trillion tokens.

demo.html: Match each job to its stage of the pre-training data pipeline.

example.html:
Chinchilla arithmetic. 70 billion parameters × 20 tokens each = 1.4 trillion tokens. Compute ≈ 6 × 70×10⁹ × 1.4×10¹² ≈ 5.9×10²³ operations. Spending the same budget on a 280-billion-parameter model leaves only 0.35 trillion tokens: the bigger model ends up worse.

Supplementary Many recent models are trained on far more than 20 tokens per parameter on purpose: a smaller model is cheaper every time it answers a question.

misunderstandings: The next token is the label.
BERT-style masking is better for chatbots.
Without enough data the model is under-trained.
Duplicates just waste a little time.
takeaways: Pre-training = self-supervised next-token prediction on huge text.
Causal LM for generation; masked LM for understanding.
Pipeline: collect → clean → deduplicate → tokenize → train.
Continuous pre-training adapts a model to a domain.
Loss is a power law in N, D, C; C ≈ 6ND; ~20 tokens per parameter.
thirty: Pre-training is self-supervised next-token prediction over a huge corpus; the loss is −ln p(correct token) (p = 0.25 → 1.39 nats). Causal LMs (GPT, Llama) predict from the left and can generate; masked LMs (BERT) fill hidden tokens from both sides for understanding. The data pipeline (collect, clean, deduplicate, tokenize) is critical; deduplication (hashing, shingle Jaccard/MinHash) prevents memorisation. BPE builds a sub-word vocabulary by merging frequent pairs. Continuous pre-training on domain text gives domain adaptation cheaply. Scaling laws: loss falls as a power law in parameters N, data D and compute C, predictably with diminishing returns. Chinchilla: balance N and D at about 20 tokens per parameter with C ≈ 6ND; 70B → 1.4T tokens → 5.9×10²³ FLOPs; grow model and data together.
